subjects.name: Tang China: a capital and its many connections
subjects.geographicPrecision: Capital locator; no claim that one city represents all Tang society.

interval.label: Tang dynastic frame, 618–907 CE
interval.note: Conventional dynasty dates; individual objects and political disruptions have their own chronology.

subjects.question: What does a tomb figure reveal about the living city?
subjects.summary: Chang’an joined court government, neighborhoods, markets and religious communities. People moved through a built environment that organized access as well as exchange. A tomb musician presents one carefully made image of courtly life; it cannot stand for the city’s whole population. The capital and its institutions changed within the Tang dynasty’s long conventional frame.

sections.title: An inherited capital needed people to make it work
sections.text: The Tang did not begin with an empty landscape. A new capital had been built under the preceding Sui, south of the earlier Han city. Rulers inherited government institutions as well as streets and buildings. Offices needed people who could read and write; the examination system offered some educated men a route into service. Access still depended on education and social position. A recruitment procedure describes one way of staffing government, rather than demonstrating that every resident could participate equally.

sections.title: Walls and gates shaped an ordinary errand
sections.text: The NUS seminar summary describes walled residential wards, gates, markets and a curfew that restricted movement. Going out for supplies therefore depended on more than distance: opening times and permission mattered. The diagram separates a ward, a public street and a market as functional settings. It gives no surveyed route or uniform house plan. The summary explicitly calls reconstructed ward interiors conjectural; their residents did not all occupy identical compounds.

sections.title: A musician is an image made for a tomb
sections.text: The earthenware figure holds an implement with ribbons or strings which the Met compares with castanets. Pigment and shaped clothing give the figure a specific visual character. Its catalogue classification is tomb pottery. Someone selected, made and placed an image of performance for a funerary setting; this is different evidence from a performer’s own testimony. The sculpture supplies neither a personal name nor a record of wages. Its seventh–eighth-century date is narrower than the whole Tang frame.

sections.title: Religious communities and government changed together
sections.text: Xuanzang returned to the capital in 645 with texts that he subsequently translated. The university account distinguishes the pagoda first built in 652 from rebuilding in 701–704. Translation and storage required sustained institutional work, beyond the moment of arrival. Different religious communities lived in the capital, but their presence did not guarantee permanent security. Persecutions in 845 and the dynasty’s continuation after a major mid-eighth-century rebellion prevent a single timeless picture of openness or stable court authority.

deeperReading.title: A city’s surviving buildings run on different clocks
deeperReading.text: The university essay carries the reader from the Han and Sui capitals to Tang religious buildings and later Ming structures. This makes a practical method: identify which phase a surviving feature belongs to before using it to picture a whole city. A building first founded in one year can contain substantial later rebuilding. Similarly, a tomb object can illuminate representation without locating its original workshop or the household of a living performer. Comparing these sources requires several dated histories, not one illustration labeled “Tang life.”

deeperReading.title: Two kinds of learning served different tasks
deeperReading.text: Compare recruiting an officeholder with translating returned scriptures. The first selects people for government service; the second makes a body of writing available through another language. Both require learned work, but sharing a capital does not make their audiences, purposes or opportunities identical. The tomb musician adds another form of skilled activity represented in the city’s wider courtly culture. Ask who could enter each setting and whose own voice survives. The comparison broadens institutional history beyond a ruler’s list of achievements.

subjects.question: Can a craft tradition spread while political unity weakens?
subjects.summary: Cities, workshops and books followed different rhythms within Abbasid-era Iraq. A bowl makes skilled surface work visible, while its unknown workshop remains a question. Baghdad’s founding, the court’s move to Samarra and later changes in political control did not make one continuous administrative system. Reading craft beside urban and scholarly institutions gives a fuller history than the dynasty label alone.

sections.title: A capital concentrated demands and opportunities
sections.text: Baghdad was founded in 762, after the Abbasids had taken power in 750. The court moved to Samarra in 836 and returned to Baghdad in 892. Building, supplying and decorating those places created work for many kinds of maker. Yet a find at a palace need not have been produced nearby or commissioned personally by a ruler. The two capitals are separate settings in a longer history, and the wider population’s work cannot be reduced to court consumption.

sections.title: The bowl’s surface required decisions and skill
sections.text: The selected tenth-century vessel is earthenware with lustre painting over an opaque white glaze. A seated man, plants and birds organize its decoration; the catalogue reads a blessing on its foot. Making such surfaces involved ingredients, skilled potters, kilns, fuel and attention, including failures. The process diagram separates the ceramic body, glazed surface and controlled lustre firing. It explains a technical task without assigning a recipe, temperature or named workshop to this accession.

sections.title: A production place needs more than a style name
sections.text: Pottery found at Samarra is not automatically pottery made there. Kiln debris and material comparisons provide different evidence from a vessel’s decoration. Petersen’s fieldwork report discusses Basra-region finds while retaining uncertainties about their original recovery and the possibility of several southern Iraqi production centers. Early Basra near al-Zubayr also differs from the modern city farther east. Neither this regional research nor the bowl’s Iraq attribution identifies the selected object’s precise workshop, owner or journey.

sections.title: Books also depended on skilled production
sections.text: A manuscript leaf attributed to Baghdad and dated 621 AH/1224 CE names ‘Abdullah ibn al-Fadl. It belongs to an Arabic version of a much older Greek treatise and combines writing with illustration. This later object makes copying, interpretation and presentation visible. Its date is not the beginning of translation into Arabic, and an illustrated setting is not an observed hospital interior. The example extends the account beyond pottery without treating every city or century as one scholarly institution.

sections.title: Political authority changed before the final date
sections.text: The caliphs’ power narrowed as other rulers gained control; Baghdad’s capture by the Buyids in 945 and Seljuqs in 1055 differs from the Mongol sack in 1258. The conventional endpoint cannot stand in for centuries of unchanged rule. Crafts, books and institutions therefore need their own dated evidence.

deeperReading.title: Ordinary pottery broadens the question
deeperReading.text: A 2022 study examined 134 selected common, generally unglazed sherds from Murwab in Qatar. Petrography addresses materials and possible origins; chemical results and provenance suggestions remain preliminary. This concerns a different settlement and different sampled pots, not chemical testing of the selected Met bowl. It shows why an account centered on a glittering museum vessel should also ask about cooking, storage and household supply. The sample does not count every pot or identify the movements of every household.

deeperReading.title: Old explanations remain questions to test
deeperReading.text: Rosser-Owen’s course discusses theories connecting costly innovation with court sponsorship and overseas trade. Petersen’s report explicitly qualifies production-center arguments and warns that collected surface sherds only indicate, rather than securely date, occupation. Keep these kinds of inference visible: a hypothesis about investment, evidence about a clay fabric and an object’s museum attribution do different work. None alone establishes who paid a potter, whether a particular worker migrated or how one vessel reached a consumer.

deeperReading.title: A century-wide object date can cross a political change
deeperReading.text: The selected bowl’s tenth-century date spans the 945 change in Baghdad’s control. That range cannot establish whether it was made before or after the takeover, still less identify a patron from the ruling dynasty. Ask what additional dating or ownership evidence would narrow the question. The manuscript’s 1224 date supplies a different degree of precision for another object and task. A dynastic label groups material for study; it cannot replace the dates and circumstances of manufacture, use and survival.

subjects.question: How can movement through a building teach an idea?
subjects.summary: Borobudur joins a built hill, carved stories and spaces for movement. Builders and carvers organized stone surfaces while upkeep linked religious institutions to resources and people. Evidence for those relationships comes from the monument, modern studies, attributed inscription interpretation and later conservation; each answers a different question.

sections.title: A building organized around a hill
sections.text: UNESCO describes five concentric square terraces below three circular platforms and a crowning stupa, built around a natural hill. Walls and balustrades carry reliefs; seventy-two openwork stupas surround the central upper stupa and change the surrounding forms. Stonework and carving therefore made both spaces to enter and surfaces to attend to. UNESCO relates the arrangement to Buddhist cosmology. A modern schematic helps distinguish its shapes, but supplies neither a measured survey nor a record of any visitor’s thoughts.

sections.title: Stories included recognizable kinds of buildings
sections.text: Hari Setyawan’s study examines wooden-building roofs represented in the reliefs. It compares forms and story settings to interpret dwellings, storage buildings, halls and monastic spaces. Those settings make practical activities part of a religious narrative world: sheltering, gathering and storing matter alongside carved figures. The study locates Lalitavistara on the upper first-gallery wall and Gandavyuha on later gallery walls. Reading a sequence means attending to a scene’s position as well as its carved content. Comparing those locations makes the relationship between a story and an architectural surface inspectable. These are interpretations of depicted architecture, not recovered floor plans or a census of the households living beside the monument.

sections.title: Moving water required continued work
sections.text: Rain falling on terraces had to leave the structure. The conservation encyclopedia describes earlier drainage through jaladwara, or water spouts, toward lower levels and the hill. It distinguishes this from pipes, infiltration wells and inspection basins introduced during the second restoration. Water disposal connects the monument’s form with recurrent inspection and repair. The 2008 photograph consequently shows a surviving conserved building; it cannot separate all early stones from twentieth-century interventions by appearance alone.

sections.title: Support reached beyond the carved stone
sections.text: Religious upkeep also needed resources. BorobudurPedia interprets the 842 Tri Tepusan inscription as land privileges supporting a religious foundation connected with Borobudur. That account offers a concrete way to ask how surrounding production could contribute to maintenance, without recovering every payment or naming a certain founder. In the present landscape, a December 2025 exhibition documented builders, carpenters, potters and other practitioners sharing local architectural knowledge. Their work gives neighboring communities a visible role today, without making their houses unchanged survivals from the construction centuries.

That convention helps locate passages for comparison; Table 1 associates galleries and walls or balustrades with narrative cycles. It does not turn the unlabelled schematic into a measured panel plan or show that every ancient visitor followed a single mandatory itinerary. A numbered research sequence and an individual’s religious experience are different questions.

deeperReading.title: Patronage needs the right document and translation
deeperReading.text: The 842 interpretation above comes from a modern institutional encyclopedia. The separately consulted Kayumwungan digital edition supplies English only for stanzas 12 and 14, not its complete Old Javanese grant section. It is also a different inscription. These limited translated stanzas cannot silently become a full Tri Tepusan translation or a secure Borobudur foundation biography. UNESCO’s broad Syailendra attribution remains distinct from identifying one patron, collecting actual revenues or recovering labor conditions.

deeperReading.title: A living landscape includes disagreement
deeperReading.text: The December 2024 monitoring mission heard vendor and resident concerns about access, relocation and benefits, and recommended further engagement. Those mediated accounts complicate any picture of a monument with one unanimous surrounding community. The later architecture exhibition documents another form of participation, not proof that every concern was resolved. Likewise, a modern Cultural Axis Path project linking the monuments cannot establish an ancient procession. Source date, purpose and the people represented remain part of the explanation.

subjects.name: Nalanda: living and learning together
subjects.geographicPrecision: Monastic archaeological-site locator; not a map of every associated learning network.

interval.label: Monastic and scholastic institution, fifth–thirteenth centuries CE
interval.note: UNESCO Brief synthesis distinguishes this institution from earlier site remains reaching the third century BCE. End expressed by century, not an exact destruction year.

subjects.question: What can rooms and repairs reveal about learning?
subjects.summary: At Nalanda, living together made learning possible. Residential buildings, worship, teaching, food and support from outside the monastery belonged to an institution that changed across centuries. Yijing’s seventh-century account makes some routines visible, through an 1896 English translation. Excavated and conserved brick remains answer different questions from that account; a modern photograph cannot show a complete ancient timetable.

sections.title: A long institutional history differs from older site remains
sections.text: UNESCO’s detailed synthesis distinguishes earlier archaeology from the monastic and scholastic establishment of the fifth–thirteenth centuries. The surviving buildings developed through construction phases rather than one founding design. Viharas provided residential and educational infrastructure beside religious buildings and shrines. Bringing these functions together allowed people to remain, learn and worship, but the excavated portion is smaller than the historical complex. Neither a protected-area boundary nor a modern university analogy defines the institution’s whole past.

sections.title: Learning required support beyond a teaching hall
sections.text: On printed page 65, Yijing’s translated account says Nalanda held lands associated with villages granted by generations of kings. This connects study with continuing support from outside the residential buildings. The passage does not describe every cultivator’s obligations or the distribution of the proceeds. Endowment is therefore a starting question about resources and dependence, not proof that all the people sustaining the monastery shared its privileges. The account’s praise of discipline also serves the author’s argument for better monastic practice.

citations.locator: Printed p. 65: Nalanda and endowed villages

sections.title: A daily practice needed coordination and other workers
sections.text: The translated account describes chanting carried from hall to hall because a large community could not assemble easily in one place. Lay assistants and children accompany the chant leader with incense and flowers. This is a concrete way to coordinate worship across several spaces, and it brings people besides senior scholars into view. Resident totals vary across the text traditions noted by the translator. These passages should not become an exact population chart or a room-by-room match with today’s excavated ruins.

sections.title: Study meant learning and explaining, not merely storing texts
sections.text: Yijing’s learning discussion moves from grammatical study toward composition, reasoning and Buddhist analysis. It names Nalanda and Valabhi as settings where students learn from teachers and instruct others. Such activity depended on skilled people who could explain and debate, rather than a collection of books alone. This selected passage is not a syllabus for every century or every resident. An account intended to explain and commend practices to distant readers also needs reading for its purpose.

sections.text: The 2023 photograph shows brick walls and openings in conserved remains. It is evidence of what a visitor could see then. deeperReading.title: Keep Tamralipti and Nalanda apart
deeperReading.text: Pages 63–64 describe room allocation, guest treatment and a teacher’s disciplinary case before page 65 identifies these as customs at Bha-ra-ha monastery in Tamralipti. The text then turns separately to Nalanda. Transferring every earlier detail to Nalanda would erase the author’s own transition. Page 154 makes another explicit move between the two settings. Identify the place named in a passage before using an attractive detail to fill a gap in an institutional story.

deeperReading.title: Translation and conservation each add an interpretive layer
deeperReading.text: Takakusu’s 1896 edition includes textual variants and explanations of terms for monastic assistants. Its wording is not a transparent recording of every seventh-century voice. Read reported observation, recommended practice and a translator’s note separately. Archaeology introduces other layers: excavation exposes parts of a changing complex, and conservation protects what survives. UNESCO calls for continued documentation of repairs. A responsible account can explain a routine while leaving the workers’ own perspectives, land arrangements and an exact room identification unresolved.

deeperReading.title: Follow support from a grant toward daily life
deeperReading.text: An endowed resource could sustain residence and learning only through continuing work and arrangements for supply. The account names generations of royal donors, while saying much less about the people producing that support. Follow the explanatory chain from a grant to resources and then to the tasks residents could perform. Its missing links matter: the selected passage does not specify every tenure agreement, payment or cultivator’s experience. Land records and evidence of provisioning would test those questions more directly than another view of a monument.

sections.title: A container joined several kinds of work
sections.text: This large ceramic cup brings making and representation together. Fine incised outlines run across its pale surface, while the catalogue proposes a painted-stucco finish near the rim. Doyle’s wider account describes Maya potters forming vessels by hand and choosing clay, additives and surfaces before firing. Such choices made containers durable and gave artists a working surface. They supply a production context for this cup, while its particular clay recipe, workshop and maker remain unrecorded.

It makes ownership a visible social relationship: a named person could be connected with a container used for serving and display. The figure and signs also share the same composition. The catalogue considers it possible that the seated figure represents the named owner; the text supplies no polity.

sections.text: Doyle relates the cup’s form to cacao preparation scenes on other vessels, where pouring makes froth. Shared dipping is a proposed reconstruction of use. The museum reads imagery of agricultural fertility as connecting the represented ruler with food and renewal. In the wider Classic-period account, finely made vessels also served as diplomatic gifts between courts and governors. Their circulation could carry skilled work and messages about relationships, without establishing a particular gift event for this cup.

Sheets describes people producing food and goods for their own use, making surplus through part-time specialties and exchanging products with neighbors or at elite centers. Groundstone tools, painted gourds and plant fibers enter that account. A later botanical study documents productive gardens and outfields. This evidence explains daily work beyond courtly imagery; it does not locate this museum cup at Cerén.

subjects.question: What is missing when a city is pictured as only a temple?
subjects.summary: Angkor was a landscape of temples, settlements, fields and water works built and altered over centuries. Stone monuments survive conspicuously; traces of less durable buildings and infrastructure require other ways of looking. Satellite observation, lidar, excavation and network models help us ask how the city worked, why it changed, and why the story cannot end with an empty jungle.

sections.title: Begin outside the famous temple
sections.text: Angkor Wat belongs to a much larger settlement landscape. UNESCO includes reservoirs, canals, roads and successive capital plans within its account of the site. The water works mattered alongside ceremonial buildings: they connected places, helped manage seasonal water and supported cultivation. Different rulers added or altered projects. A modern visitor sees remains from many phases together, so the visible landscape must not be mistaken for a single design built in one reign. Our map separates several locations to make those relationships easier to investigate.

sections.title: How a water network works
sections.text: Reservoirs store water; channels move it; embankments and control points influence where it goes. The 2018 study describes a system serving flood regulation and agriculture, accumulated through repeated construction and modification. Connections matter as much as individual structures. A reservoir cannot supply a place if its connecting channel no longer functions. Maintenance is therefore part of urban history: excavation, clearing and repair are recurring work, not just the exceptional achievement of building a monument. Religious and political importance does not remove these material demands.

citations.locator: Angkor’s water distribution network; modeling framework

sections.title: Seeing traces beneath vegetation
sections.text: Many buildings were made of perishable materials, leaving subtler traces than stone temples. The 2013 lidar study used airborne laser scanning to model ground surfaces beneath vegetation. Roads, ponds, occupation mounds and organized layouts became easier to recognize. Lidar does not directly show the people who once lived there or tell us the year of every feature. It changes what can be mapped, then archaeology has to connect those forms to activities and dates. A seemingly isolated temple can become part of a much larger urban pattern.

citations.locator: Introduction; airborne laser scanning and urban landscapes

sections.title: Stress can travel through connections
sections.text: Penny and colleagues tested a model derived from archaeological mapping. At a branching channel, stronger flow can erode one branch and attract still more water. Another branch receives less, deposits sediment and loses capacity. In the model, sufficiently large disturbances can produce cascading changes elsewhere in the network. This is a possible mechanism linking unusual water flows to infrastructure damage. It does not reproduce every historical decision or establish that water damage alone caused political change. The authors argue for a contributing vulnerability, in combination with climatic variation.

sections.title: Transformation did not empty the landscape
sections.text: The history of particular places complicates a single abandonment date. Excavations around Angkor Wat found changing occupation of its habitation mounds, while inscriptions and modifications attest to the temple’s continuing importance. Political relocation, religious change, trade and climate belong in the discussion together. UNESCO also describes villages and cultivation in the present heritage landscape. The end of a capital phase is not the end of everyone’s relationship with a place. Asking what continued is as important as asking what failed.

deeperReading.title: A mechanism is not a complete cause
deeperReading.text: A model is valuable because it makes assumptions explicit enough to test. Here channels become connections in a network, and changing flow alters their capacities through erosion and sedimentation. That abstraction allows researchers to examine how local change might spread. It also leaves out much of social life: who organized repairs, how communities responded, and how political priorities changed. The historical interpretation is strongest when the modeled mechanism is tested against independently dated archaeological and environmental evidence. It is weaker if the model is retold as a witnessed sequence of events.

deeperReading.title: Four instruments, four questions
deeperReading.text: The satellite image is a modern view of surface patterns. Lidar models ground elevation and exposes subtle forms beneath vegetation. Excavation investigates deposits and material remains in selected places. A network model tests the behavior of a simplified system. These approaches complement one another precisely because they do different work. Seeing a rectangular reservoir from space does not date its construction; finding an occupation layer does not map every household. Begin with the question, then choose the evidence suited to answering it.

deeperReading.title: Do not turn 1431 into an on/off switch
deeperReading.text: The Angkor Wat study places local changes within a much longer sequence and cautions against treating conventional political chronology as a universal date of abandonment. People could leave one precinct, continue worship at another and alter the use of surrounding mounds. Our broad ninth–fifteenth-century frame organizes a capital-era investigation; it is not a claim that the settlement was created in 800 or emptied in 1500. Continuing communities belong to the history of the place, not only to an epilogue about modern tourism.

subjects.question: Can objects and paintings embody competing views of an ordered world?
subjects.summary: Song institutions joined court service, commercial activity and skilled production. A tea bowl makes material work visible; a proposal about crop loans exposes a different relationship between officials and farming households. Neither stands for everyone’s experience. Northern and Southern Song had different capital settings, while neighboring states and changing borders prevent a single unchanging picture of China.

sections.title: A bowl begins with work, rather than a dynasty label
sections.text: This Jian-ware bowl is stoneware with a dark, streaked glaze conventionally called hare’s fur. Its catalogue date is the eleventh–twelfth century, a range spanning more than one political phase. Forming a vessel and controlling its fired surface required practical skill. The photograph shows a finished object; it does not identify its potter, fuel supply, purchaser or a shipment to the capital. A name for a ware is not a complete workshop history.

sections.title: Market exchange depended on other people’s tasks
sections.text: The Columbia teaching account describes markets spreading through cities and the countryside, specialized producers and water transport for bulky goods such as grain. Growing for sale linked a household’s choices to buyers and prices. Boats still needed loading, routes and provisioning. Commercial activity therefore involved several kinds of work, beyond making a fine bowl. The presence of markets does not by itself establish that every cultivator became wealthier or had equal bargaining power.

sections.title: A proposal tried to alter the timing of debt
sections.text: In the 1069 crop-loan memorial, the fiscal commission proposed using public reserves to lend before harvest and accept repayment with later tax instalments. It also described buying grain when prices were low and selling when high to moderate price swings. For a household, receiving resources before a crop was ready could matter as much as an annual total. This is the policy’s stated rationale. Whether officials made borrowing voluntary, and how repayment worked after poor harvests, require evidence beyond the proposal.

sections.title: Court culture did not exhaust government
sections.text: The Met essay contrasts imperial painting patronage with scholar-official expression. Such cultural differences help explain competing ideals, but offices also collected taxes, kept records and provisioned military forces. Hartman argues that accounts focused only on elite literati leave other political workers out. Read the bowl, a court ideal and a fiscal proposal together without making them interchangeable evidence. A ceramic surface cannot tell us whether a named loan was repaid.

sections.text: The conventional Northern Song frame ends in 1127, when the court lost its northern capital to the Jurchen Jin. Southern Song government was centered at Hangzhou; it ended with the Mongol conquest in 1279. These transitions changed political geography. They did not make a bowl’s broad date exact or turn the whole region into one uninterrupted jurisdiction.

Loans used reserves to address a seasonal shortage, then brought repayment into an official collection cycle. It also allowed delay after disaster. deeperReading.title: Who appears in a history of government?
deeperReading.text: Hartman’s introduction reviews sharply different modern interpretations of Song governance. His own argument broadens attention to clerks and military officials, as well as the monarch and literati. This is an interpretive intervention, not a settled vote among historians. It prompts a practical question: whose work disappears when the surviving voices belong mostly to highly educated officials? A household budget or a clerk’s register could answer questions that a painting or policy defense leaves open.

subjects.question: What connects a stone building, a traded ingredient and a living cultural landscape?
subjects.summary: Chaco’s buildings required stonework, timber, food and repeated care. Great houses, smaller habitation compounds and constructed alignments reveal different scales of work. Their institutional meaning remains debated, while a dated Pueblo council statement makes continuing relationships with the landscape explicit.

sections.title: Materials made different spaces possible
sections.text: Rows of stones and wood spanning openings are visible in the supplied Pueblo Bonito photograph. The NPS architectural account describes great-house walls built with rubble cores and carefully coursed outer masonry. These were different parts of a construction, not simply a decorated flat surface. Builders also arranged rooms, plazas and circular spaces. Pueblo Bonito’s staged construction frame stretches approximately 850–1150 CE: making a large building involved successive work rather than one completed moment. The photograph cannot date every part or name its builders.

Architecture: great houses and core/veneer construction

sections.title: Smaller houses belong beside the monuments
sections.text: The same NPS account describes smaller habitation sites with storage rooms, pithouses, outdoor shelters and later room additions. Such spaces place keeping supplies and carrying out household activities beside monumental construction. Their smaller scale matters: a great house should not stand in for every home in the canyon. NPS discusses the great houses as possible public architecture used for gathering and ceremony. That interpretation opens a question about how residents and visitors shared work; it does not recover every room’s function or choose one settled government model.

sections.title: Food connected fields, storage and gathering
sections.text: People living and gathering in this landscape needed food as well as buildings. The NPS subsistence account discusses rainfall variation, stored plant remains and water-control features. It presents competing explanations for the balance between local cultivation and supplies brought from outside. Directing seasonal water, keeping crops and preparing food were practical tasks; their precise scale and organization remain questions. A material found in selected vessels can document an ingredient, while evidence for staple farming must address different fields, samples and environmental conditions.

sections.title: Built connections have more than one possible use
sections.text: Carved steps, masonry stairways and ramps show work invested in moving through the landscape. NPS also explains that many identified road segments do not form a demonstrably continuous route. Some may have had ceremonial or symbolic roles alongside practical uses. New construction and Chaco’s regional role changed in the 1100s and 1200s; this does not end Pueblo histories. A 2025 All Pueblo Council of Governors resolution describes continuing spiritual, historical and cultural significance. It is an attributed statement of living relationships, not proof that every person endorses one archaeological explanation.

deeperReading.title: A photograph contains preservation history
deeperReading.text: The surviving walls need care after exposure. NPS describes water, freeze–thaw cycles and lost roofs or plaster as causes of deterioration. Modern treatment can include mortar repair, replacement stones, capping and backfilling. Its account also documents local Navajo crews working in the late 1930s preservation programme. These are skilled activities with their own dates. They make the present photograph useful evidence of a conserved structure, without letting us classify every visible stone as ancient or modern by appearance alone.

deeperReading.title: A small chemical sample does not become a universal menu
deeperReading.text: The retained Crown and Hurst consultation records five vessel-fragment samples from Pueblo Bonito. Three probable cylinder-jar samples yielded theobromine, interpreted as cacao evidence; stylistic dating places the sherds around 1000–1125 CE. This supports an ingredient-use inference and raises questions about preparation and movement. It does not identify all intermediaries, an exact route, every household’s access or the main source of staple calories. The study’s separately copyrighted vessel figure is not reproduced.

deeperReading.title: Institutional descriptions need named perspectives
deeperReading.text: A gathering place, a redistribution centre and a political centre are interpretations that call for different evidence. They need not explain every structure or century alike. The council resolution contributes another kind of record: a dated statement that Greater Chaco remains culturally significant. Reading it alongside archaeological questions neither makes contemporary peoples disappear at a timeline boundary nor treats them as unanimous witnesses to one reconstruction. Fuller specialist and community review remains necessary.

packs.title: Communities and institutions in transition
packs.question: How did institutions, beliefs and regional networks change after political transitions?
packs.orientation: Large political labels contain changing communities. Investigate how people made images, shared food, organized learning and built religious environments while political power shifted.
packs.geography: Capitals on the Bosporus, Tigris and in northern China sit beside Mesoamerican vessel traditions, South Asian monastic life and Central Javanese architecture. Chaco’s mid/late-ninth-century building context provides a distinct Southwestern case extending into the next chapter.
packs.limits: Western Europe beyond Byzantium, inland Africa, North America and many smaller communities need fuller treatment. The selected cases do not define one universal medieval stage.

Americas.reason: Maya text/food/rank and earlier Andean/Mexican contexts now include the beginning of Chaco’s regional building history. Most northern regions remain unrepresented.

orientations.title: Maya households and the beginnings of Chaco great houses
orientations.question: How can we compare work without making different communities contemporary by assumption?

summary.title: Courtly containers and village provision
summary.text: The selected Maya cup connects a named owner with food and imagery. Excavated Cerén households offer a different view: food production, part-time specialties and exchange. These settings bring makers and household provision into a history otherwise easily dominated by courtly objects.

sections.title: Building over generations
sections.text: Farther north, Pueblo Bonito was constructed in stages from about 850 to 1150 CE. Its rooms and masonry are the accumulated results of work over generations. A photograph of the whole structure therefore cannot show what stood at the beginning of construction.

sections.title: Objects and buildings keep different clocks
sections.text: The Maya cup’s seventh–eighth-century catalogue date precedes the 850 CE snapshot. The Chaco cacao study’s sampled vessels are later, around 1000–1125. Comparing their evidence is useful, but neither supplies a documented cacao-drinking event at Chaco in 850 or a route taken by this Maya vessel.

orientations.scope: A comparison of Maya court/village evidence and an Ancestral Puebloan building sequence. Neither is a summary of all American communities; the objects and deposits do not share one date.
orientations.perspectives: Courtly writing names an owner. Household archaeology and building remains reveal other tasks, while often leaving individual workers unnamed.

activity.prompt: Could a photograph of completed Pueblo Bonito illustrate the site as it looked in 850 CE?
activity.response: Use it to introduce the conserved site, with a clear caption. Reconstructing 850 requires evidence for the earliest building phases; the complete later footprint cannot be backdated.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE marks the approximate beginning of Pueblo Bonito’s staged construction, not completion of the great house. The selected Maya cup is earlier; the sampled Chaco cacao vessels are later. Their comparison does not establish an exchange between those particular objects or communities in this year.

orientations.title: Middle Niger towns and earlier Aksumite work
orientations.question: Must a town begin with a palace or a foreign trading expedition?

summary.title: Djenné-Djeno and its neighbours
summary.text: Excavations and settlement survey place Djenné-Djeno’s growth within the first millennium CE, with a high point around 750–1100. Nearby settlements were part of this urban landscape. This history precedes the Mali Empire explored in the linked dossier; the later royal map cannot explain the origins of these towns.

sections.title: Food and materials connected settlements
sections.text: The excavation report considers rice, fish and other local products alongside imported stone and iron. Urban exchange depended on supplies from a wider landscape, not only conspicuous imported luxuries. Its account challenges the idea that Middle Niger towns arose solely as an effect of later trans-Saharan trade.

citations.locator: Extract: staples, imported materials and interpretation

sections.title: An earlier eastern comparison
sections.text: Beta Samati in the Aksumite highlands preserves food preparation and small-scale production in separately dated deposits. This provides an earlier comparison for urban work, not a second African town established as occupied in 850 by those deposits. The two regions should not be forced into one sequence of rise and decline.

sections.title: Different town, different surviving fabric
sections.text: The UNESCO property includes Djenné-Djeno and other archaeological sites alongside the fabric of present Djenné. Later Islamic architecture must remain separate from the earlier settlement evidence. Buildings visible today are not automatically a picture of the ninth century.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: component sites and later town

orientations.scope: A Middle Niger focus with an explicitly earlier Horn comparison. The 1981 excavation report is consulted through its published extract, not a new analysis of all underlying finds. No continent-wide political model is inferred.
orientations.perspectives: Household remains and regional survey broaden the account beyond rulers. They do not recover every resident’s voice or prove that social differences were absent.

activity.prompt: Which evidence would help distinguish a town supported by its hinterland from a story based only on imported treasures?
activity.response: Look for local food production, ordinary tools, settlement relationships and dated exchange evidence. Explain what imported material adds without treating it as the sole cause of urban life.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE lies within the excavation report’s 750–1100 high point for Djenné-Djeno and nearby settlements. This supplies a Middle Niger urban setting before the later Mali Empire. Aksumite deposits and the architecture of present Djenné retain their separate chronologies.

orientations.title: Aachen and Constantinople: buildings, images and changing authority
orientations.question: How can a building preserve several different political and religious moments?

summary.title: Two court settings
summary.text: Aachen’s palace chapel formed part of Charlemagne’s residence. Constantinople combined imperial and church institutions with craft production. Comparing them draws attention to the ways built spaces and images helped present authority; it does not make their governments or communities identical.

sections.title: Working with material and inherited forms
sections.text: Aachen’s octagonal core, galleries and bronze fittings bring skilled construction into the story. In Constantinople, the linked dossier distinguishes ivory carving from the fitting and repair of excavated ships. A courtly building or luxury object required work, but does not alone disclose each worker’s status.

sections.title: Later additions change what a visitor sees
sections.text: Aachen’s chapel was subsequently enlarged, and its present dome mosaic dates to 1880–1881. At Constantinople, disputes over religious images preceded the restoration of icons in 843. The selected tenth-century ivory is later than that transition; its date cannot be moved back to illustrate the precise moment.

orientations.scope: Two selected court and religious settings, not all of Europe. Aachen’s source offers overlapping early construction formulations; neither supplies a day-by-day schedule. No claim of a uniform European revival is adopted.
orientations.perspectives: Royal patronage and surviving religious objects are prominent; shipbuilding and material work expose additional activities without documenting all households.

activity.prompt: Which parts of a present-day building can safely be used to describe an earlier century?
activity.response: Identify separately dated fabric, later additions and restoration. Keep uncertain features labelled; a building’s foundation date is not the date of every visible element.

snapshots.text: By 850 CE Aachen’s early ninth-century chapel had been built, while Constantinople stood shortly after the 843 restoration of icons. The present Aachen mosaic and the selected Byzantine ivory belong to later dates and do not illustrate this exact year.

orientations.title: Baghdad, Samarra and the work of Abbasid workshops
orientations.question: What changes when a court moves but skilled production continues?

summary.title: Cities with separate histories
summary.text: Baghdad was founded in 762; the Abbasid court was based at Samarra from 836 to 892. Their surviving evidence differs. Samarra’s remains are particularly important because early Abbasid Baghdad is less well preserved, rather than because one city contained all regional creativity.

citations.locator: Opening capital chronology and survival paragraphs

sections.title: A finished surface required repeated work
sections.text: Lustre-painted pottery required investment in materials, fuel, skilled handling and firing. The Ashmolean account considers production centres and patronage as questions, not a settled identification of one inventor or workshop for every vessel. The selected bowl’s surface can begin an investigation without supplying its maker’s name.

sections.title: Political authority and craft have different endpoints
sections.text: During the tenth century, local dynasties gained greater autonomy and Abbasid control changed. That political history does not establish that ceramic skill or book production ended everywhere. Objects, workshops, court residence and wider authority each need their own dated evidence.

citations.locator: Tenth-century political changes and later book production

orientations.scope: A justified focus on two Iraqi capitals and their production questions. No universal Islamic culture, precise trade itinerary or single birthplace of a technique is inferred.
orientations.perspectives: Court commissions and museum collections preserve selected products. Kiln work and costly failures draw attention to makers, whose own accounts remain scarce.

activity.prompt: Does a court’s departure date establish the date when all workshops in that city closed?
activity.response: No. Compare workshop deposits, dated products and other production records with the court chronology. Administrative change alone does not date each working place.

snapshots.text: In 850 CE the Abbasid court was in Samarra, within its 836–892 residence there. Baghdad’s founding in 762 and later changes in caliphal power are distinct events. A vessel’s broader catalogue range does not make it a documented product of this exact year.

orientations.title: Nalanda and Paharpur: sustaining places of learning
orientations.question: What work made a residential learning community possible?

summary.title: Two monastic settings
summary.text: Nalanda in Bihar and Paharpur in present-day Bangladesh bring residences, religious buildings and learning into one inquiry. Nalanda’s institutional history spans the fifth–thirteenth centuries; Paharpur’s foundation is associated with Dharmapala around the late eighth–early ninth century. Their buildings accumulated in phases.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: foundation and building phases

sections.title: Learning needed food, rooms and people
sections.text: Yijing’s seventh-century account describes support and routines at Nalanda, as well as teaching and explanation. At Paharpur, the archaeological description identifies kitchens and a refectory as well as cells and a shrine. These sources make provisioning part of institutional history, while answering different questions about daily life.

sections.title: An account is not a plan of every phase
sections.text: Yijing’s translated description cannot be matched room for room to Nalanda’s conserved ruins. Nor can Paharpur’s final count of cells be assumed for its foundation. Successive construction and documented repairs mean that a single plan can combine evidence from different times.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: cells in the last building phases

orientations.scope: Two eastern monastic institutions, not all South Asian education or agriculture. Support from outside institutions is considered without inventing village routes, universal access or the experiences of every cultivator.
orientations.perspectives: Institutional and monastic accounts foreground learned residents and patrons. Food workers, cultivators and people excluded from residence are less directly represented.

activity.prompt: Why should a final building plan and an earlier visitor’s account be compared rather than treated as identical?
activity.response: State each source’s date and purpose. Seek phase-specific evidence before identifying rooms or populations; describe support and routines without equating a later footprint with an earlier census.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE falls within Nalanda’s monastic history and after the foundation period attributed to Paharpur. The complete later layouts are not securely dated to this year, and Yijing’s seventh-century observations remain earlier testimony.

orientations.title: Chang’an, Gyeongju and Nara: connected but distinct settings
orientations.question: How can shared forms coexist with different political histories?

summary.title: More than one capital
summary.text: Tang Chang’an, Silla Gyeongju and Nara preserve different combinations of court, religious and urban evidence. Nara’s monuments record links with China and Korea; Gyeongju’s palace and temple remains establish a Korean setting in its own right. Similar forms do not make one place a copy of another.

citations.locator: Brief synthesis: Wolseong and temple belts

sections.title: Institutions organized movement and work
sections.text: The Chang’an reading describes neighbourhood gates, recruitment and translation as different forms of organized activity. At Nara, audience halls, residences and religious compounds served distinct purposes. Those arrangements raise questions about access and service, without proving that every rule was followed or every resident enjoyed equal standing.

sections.title: A capital’s move does not erase a place
sections.text: Nara’s capital period ended in 784. Its temples and shrines had histories beyond that political role, including the protection of the Kasugayama sacred forest from 841 described by UNESCO. The Korean chronology separately places Silla and Barhae alongside one another, then later political transitions. These changes cannot be collapsed into Tang’s 907 endpoint.

citations.locator: Timeline: Silla, Barhae and later regimes

orientations.scope: Selected Chinese, Korean and Japanese urban/religious settings. The label Unified Silla does not erase contemporary Barhae or establish one unchanging border; neither chronology supplies all East Asian experience.
orientations.perspectives: Elite tombs and monumental compounds dominate surviving displays. Administrative functions identify work without preserving every servant, artisan or visitor’s story.

activity.prompt: Can a place still matter after it stops being the capital?
activity.response: Distinguish political residence from religious, productive and community uses. Use Nara’s earlier capital dates and later sacred-forest evidence as separate examples; do not infer abandonment from a capital move.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE lies within Tang and Silla histories, while Barhae also existed. Nara was no longer Japan’s capital, but its religious landscape continued; UNESCO dates the Kasugayama forest prohibition from 841. The selected earlier Tang tomb figure retains its own catalogue date.

orientations.title: Central Java, early Angkor and a separate Tongan sequence
orientations.question: How do we compare monument building with settlement that leaves different traces?

summary.title: Religious landscapes in Java and Cambodia
summary.text: Borobudur belongs to an eighth–ninth-century construction frame in Central Java, alongside the associated Mendut and Pawon temples. Angkor’s wider archaeological landscape includes several capitals, temples and water structures accumulated over centuries. It is not one construction project with a single completion date.

sections.title: Building and upkeep were different tasks
sections.text: Carved stone, galleries and drainage made Borobudur a working built environment. The linked reading separates construction evidence from interpretations of religious upkeep in inscriptions. Modern repairs add another phase. Neither a later charter nor a restored surface supplies a complete account of the original workforce.

sections.title: An island comparison without an invented route
sections.text: Research at Tongan sites describes settlement continuing into later periods without pottery manufacture. That makes an instructive comparison: the end of a material tradition need not mean the end of a community. It does not connect Tonga to these particular temple projects or establish a precisely dated 850 CE floor.

sections.title: The famous later monument is not the early landscape
sections.text: Angkor’s ninth-century regional beginnings should not be illustrated as though the later Angkor Wat temple already existed. Borobudur’s broad construction dates likewise do not establish which relief or terrace was finished in 850. Each monument needs its own chronology within the regional comparison.

orientations.scope: Separate Javanese, Cambodian and Tongan histories. No mainland–Pacific voyage is inferred; the Oceanian evidence is settlement continuity at sampled sites rather than a dated event in the snapshot year.
orientations.perspectives: Monumental evidence favours religious patrons and skilled stone work. Tongan settlement evidence brings a different material record into view but does not recover every resident’s experience.

activity.prompt: Does the disappearance of pottery prove that a community left its settlement?
activity.response: Look for independently dated evidence of later occupation. Explain the distinction between a material practice ending and people leaving; do not infer a replacement population from missing pots alone.

snapshots.text: Around 850 CE lies within Borobudur’s broad construction frame and the opening centuries of the Angkor regional frame. Later Angkor Wat is not backdated. The Tongan study separately documents continuity into aceramic periods, without identifying an event exactly in 850.
